ety.text: Old French -ainder. Middle English -an English -an English pedestrian From Latin pedester (oblique stem pedestri-) + English -an.

senses.d: Of or intended for those who are walking.

ex: His manner of dress was pedestrian but tidy.

senses.d: Pertaining to ordinary, everyday movements incorporated in postmodern dance.
A walker; one who walks or goes on foot, especially as opposed to one who uses a vehicle.
An expert or professional walker or runner; one who performs feats of walking or running.

grp.label: somebody walking rather than using a vehicle

ety.text: From Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”) from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moyn-is (“held in common”).
Inherited from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”), derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Compare French pion. Doublet of peone, borrowed from Spanish peón.

Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Late Latin peditō French piéter Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Frankishinflu. Old French -on Middle French -on French -on French piétonbor.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese peon, an early semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pedōnem (“one who goes on foot”), from Latin pēs (“foot”). Compare Galician peón, Spanish peón, French pion, Italian pedone.

chain.g: a hymn, especially a victory hymn, to Apollo or another god
a chant or song, especially a thanksgiving or victory hymn, to Apollo under the name Παιᾱ́ν (Paiā́n)

ety.text: From Latin paeān (“a hymn, especially a victory hymn, to Apollo or another god”), from Ancient Greek παιᾱ́ν (paiā́n, “a chant or song, especially a thanksgiving or victory hymn, to Apollo under the name Παιᾱ́ν (Paiā́n)”), from the phrase Ἰὼ Παιᾱ́ν (Iṑ Paiā́n, “O Paean!, Thanks to Paean!”).
Italian pedalebor. French pédalebor. English pedal Borrowed from French pédale, itself borrowed from Italian pedale, from Latin pedālis. By surface analysis, ped- + -al.
Latin pedālislbor. English pedal Learned borrowing from Latin pedālis. Cognate with French pédal (doublet of the pédale mentioned in § Etymology 1). Same surface analysis as in § Etymology 1.

senses.d: A lever operated by one's foot that is used to control or power a machine or mechanism, such as a bicycle or piano.
ex: There are three pedals on manual cars, two on automatics.
A piano usually has two or three pedals.

senses.d: an orthopedic structure or a footlike part.
An effects unit, especially one designed to be activated by being stepped on.
The ranks of pipes played from the pedal-board of an organ.
ex: A small organ commonly has only one or two ranks on the pedal.

senses.d: To operate a pedal attached to a wheel in a continuous circular motion.

ex: He was out of breath from pedalling up the steep hill.
The old man's backside fizgigged with laughter. "See ya, kid!" he called as Dave pedaled away.

senses.d: Of or relating to the foot.

grp.label: of or relating to the foot

senses.d: Of or pertaining to pediatrics, the branch of medicine dealing with the care and treatment of children and adolescents.
ex: The hospital has established a pediatric intensive care unit.
Currently, there are nine pediatric cases of AIDS diagnosed in Massachusetts, of whom three are attending school.
